33218-a-top-floor-idyl:
George Van Schaick's idyl tells of life on a top floor, where a night alarm, an infant, and a bolt on a door set small dramas in motion. Copyrighted in 1917, its chapters move from Frieda the angel and watching an infant to Gordon's help and further household turns. The tale is set among neighbors in close quarters, where kindness and trouble pass quickly from room to room.

Van Schaick, known for Sweetapple Cove, writes with a gentle, domestic humor, finding charm in everyday care. The book's idyllic tone suits readers who like quiet stories of home, friendship, and new life. It is a short, warm novel, best read as a series of small scenes that build into a portrait of a household and its people.
45042-a-mock-idyl:
Percy Ross's A Mock Idyl was first serialized in Longman's Magazine in 1886, and later reprinted as filler in the Favorite Library edition of Little Golden's Daughter. Nine chapters tell the story, from The Praise of Friendship through Arletta of Falaise and The Goddess to The Girl I Left Behind Me. The idyl is mock because its heroes are schoolboys and sailors, not shepherds.

Chapter one praises a friendship. Tregurtha, a Cornishman as his name declares, and Louis Roscoria shared a room at their dame's school, did each other's lessons, wore each other's hats, and took each other's floggings. Dick cut his cables and ran away to sea, urged on by his younger friend. Small Roscoria saw him off, exchanged pocket-knives, then lay on the grass howling, and was caned for refusing to tell where Tregurtha had gone. The friendship, grounded on such services, was never broken.
51103-a-chautauqua-idyl:
A Chautauqua Idyl, a prose tale by Grace Livingston, was copyrighted in 1887 by D Lothrop Company of Boston. Edward Everett Hale writes an introductory letter to the publisher. He praises the little book for telling, very simply, the story of the working out of the plan. The plan is the Chautauqua reading circle, by which grown people studied at home in set courses.

Hale hopes the older members of the circles will find grains of profit in the tale, hidden grains, none the worse for being found slowly. Livingston, he says, understood the spirit of the movement. The story opens in a rocky pasture where a brook runs tinkling over bright pebbles. Ferns grow at the water's edge, and violets nestle up the mossy bank. In the distance the lake shimmers, framed by wooded hills.
57167-my-japanese-wife-a-japanese-idyl:
My Japanese Wife, A Japanese Idyl, is a novel by Clive Holland, issued in a second edition in New York. Copyright was taken in nineteen hundred two, and Holland's earlier tale Mousme is named among his works. A picture shows Mousme and Cyril, the pair at the book's heart. Holland dedicates the edition to the real Mousme with his love, a claim that blurs tale and life.

Sixty thousand copies of prior editions had been called for, the introduction boasts in round terms. The idyl follows an Englishman's marriage to a Japanese wife in the treaty port world. Such tales fed a Western craze for Japan in those years. Charm and cultural gap carry the romance, in period terms.
66367-jenny-a-village-idyl:
M A Curtois wrote a village idyl published at London in 1890, with a motto from John Inglesant: nothing but the infinite pity is sufficient for the infinite pathos of human life. Contents open in the train, then in the village. A Rantan follows, a dialect word the next chapter explains through the home that was rantanned. An adventure in the night and the next morning build the tale.

Tim gets a chapter, then a morning call and the farm. The farmer's daughter and a class meeting continue. The return of the father ends the Rantan thread. Curtois had written Elf Knights and Tracked. Eden, Remington published the idyl at Covent Garden.
66517-a-tragic-idyl:
Tragic Idyl is a novel by Paul Bourget, published by Downey and Company in London in 1896. Bourget is named as author of Outre Mer on the title page. Contents list twelve chapters, from Le Tout Europe and The Cry of a Soul to The Denouement. 

Chapter one opens at the Casino at Monte Carlo on a night toward the end of February. A vast crowd throngs the halls of the casino in that first scene. Such nights, the narrator says, transfigure a place vulgar with the brutal luxury of its usual crowd. A sudden afflux of composite humanity gives the rooms a gay madness for the evening. On that stage Bourget sets his idyl of lovers, scruples, and a secret marriage, the chapter Il Matrimonio Segreto in the list. His novels of conscience made him the anatomist of the fashionable soul in France.
britannica-1911-beryl:
Beryl is a mineral made of beryllium and aluminium in silicate form. Its formula is given as Be3Al2Si6O18 in the 1911 Britannica article. The species includes the emerald and the aquamarine. Other clear kinds are grouped as precious beryl. Coarse kinds, unfit for gems, belong to the species too. Pliny already guessed the link between emerald and beryl, the entry notes.

Beryl forms hexagonal crystals, usually long six-sided prisms. Its colour runs blue, green, yellow, brown, or rarely pink. Some crystals are colourless. Hardness is 7.5 to 8, soft for a gem stone. The article lists finds from Royalston in Massachusetts to Mount Antero in Colorado. A Grafton crystal weighed over two and a half tons. Weathering can turn beryl into kaolin and mica.
britannica-1911-chrysoberyl:
Chrysoberyl is a yellow or green gemstone noted for its hardness, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its makeup and traits. Only diamond and corundum surpass it in hardness. Its name hints that it was once seen as a golden kind of beryl, and it does share the element beryllium with beryl.

The entry gives its chemistry in plain terms as an aluminate of beryllium, with iron held to cause the green tint. It warns that the stone is often confused with chrysolite, and then sets the two side by side by hardness, weight, and makeup. A cloudy, shimmering form of the stone is named cymophane.
britannica-1911-idyl:
Idyl is a short poem of country life, in which the feel of the landscape is kept. The 1911 Britannica article takes the word from a Greek term for a small piece in a given style. Old critics used it for many kinds of brief, plain poems. The country sense grew with the Alexandrian school of the third century BC. Theocritus, Bion, and Moschus are its great names.

Even then, the piece argues, no poet used the word as the name of a fixed form. It meant no more than a little piece in the goatherd style, or in any style named. We hold ten idyls of Theocritus, and they set the type in the mind of most readers. Yet the ten vary so much that the poet can have meant no set pattern. His dirge for Daphnis became the model of elegy, not of the idyl.
